## Course Description

Preparation for calculus: polynomial, absolute value, radical, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions and their graphs; analytic geometry, polar coordinates

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Course Content

1.  Functions including linear, polynomial, rational, radical, exponential, absolute value, logarithmic, trigonometric; definitions, evaluation, domain and range;
2.  Inverses of functions;
3.  Algebra of functions;
4.  Graphs of functions including asymptotic behavior, intercepts, and vertices;
5.  Transformations of quadratic, absolute value, radical, rational, logarithmic, exponential functions;
6.  Equations including rational, linear, radical, polynomial, exponential, trigonometric, logarithmic, and absolute value;
7.  Linear, nonlinear, and absolute value inequalities;
8.  Systems of equations and inequalities;
9.  Characterization of real and complex zeros of polynomials;
10. Unit circle and right triangle trigonometry;
11. Trigonometric and inverse trigonometric identities and formulas;
12. Graphing trigonometric functions: period, amplitude, phase shift, inverse trigonometric functions; and
13. Polar coordinates
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Course Objectives

Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:

1.  Graph functions and relations in rectangular coordinates and polar coordinates;
2.  Synthesize results from the graphs and/or equations of functions and relations;
3.  Apply transformations to the graphs of functions and relations;
4.  Recognize the relationship between functions and their inverses graphically and algebraically;
5.  Solve and apply equations including rational, linear, polynomial, exponential, absolute value, radical, and logarithmic, and solve linear, nonlinear, and absolute value inequalities;
6.  Solve systems of equations and inequalities;
7.  Apply functions to model real world applications;
8.  Identify special triangles and their related angle and side measures;
9.  Evaluate the trigonometric function of an angle given in degree and radian measure;
10. Manipulate and simplify a trigonometric expression;
11. Solve trigonometric equations, triangles, and applications;
12. Graph the basic trigonometric functions and apply changes in period, phase and amplitude to generate new graphs; and
13. Prove trigonometric identities
:::

## Connections to Data Science: Functions
Precalculus provides a foundation for data science, machine learning, and AI by helping students understand how functions describe relationships in data. Students evaluate functions, work with graphs, compare linear and nonlinear relationships, and study exponential and logarithmic functions—tools that support modeling and prediction. Connecting these topics to explanatory and response variables, scatterplots, and data modeling gives students practice interpreting graphs and using models to make and assess predictions. These connections show how Precalculus prepares students to study data science and the mathematical ideas behind machine learning and AI.


## Goals

1.  Explain how functions can be introduced as models of data.
2.  Connect the idea of input/output to explanatory/response variables.
3.  Use real data sets to compare different function models.
4.  Discuss limitations of using mathematical models for predictions.

## Activity

### Introduction
In Precalculus, we describe a function as a rule that assigns each input exactly one output. In data science, we can view functions as a model. A model is a simplified representation of data that describes patterns and allows us to make predictions.

In this lesson we will be using the [Fish Market data set]( https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/vipullrathod/fish-market). This data set includes seven fish species and measurements such as their weight, length, height, and width. In this activity, students can use the physical features of the fish as input variables to predict a fish’s weight. This could be useful for fishermen, where measuring a fish’s length or width may be easier than weighing it. Students can compare linear and polynomial models to see which better represents the relationship between a fish’s measurements and its weight.

We also introduce the idea that real data does not always have perfect linear patterns, such as a fish that may gain weight faster than the length increases. We can then discuss how nonlinear models may be helpful in describing different types of patterns in data.


### Part 1: Which function fits the fish?

Students compare linear, quadratic, power, and exponential models for predicting fish weight from length. Instructors discuss how visual fit, residual plots, and context guide model choice.

Can we estimate the weight of a fish based on its other physical features?

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| output: false

```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof input_species = Inputs.select(["Perch", "Bream", "Roach", "Pike", "Smelt", "Parkki", "Whitefish"])

```

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|  - input_species
fish |> 
  filter(Species == input_species) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = 
           aes(x = Length1, 
               y = Weight)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Scatterplot of Weight and Length of Fish",
    x = "Length (cm)",
    y = "Weight (grams)"
  )
```

We can begin with only two variables where `x = length`, and `y = weight`. We can show students a scatterplot of fish length vs. weight for different species of fish. We can then have a discussion about the plot.

1.  What do you notice about the relationship between length and weight? 

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Answer
There appears to be a nonlinear relationship.

:::

2.  Is the relationship linear? Is it a function?
3.  "Does the relationship change depending on species? What do you notice is different?"

### Part 2: Now we can fit a linear model to our scatterplots and discuss what we notice.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof input_species2 = Inputs.select(["Perch", "Bream", "Roach", "Pike", "Smelt", "Parkki", "Whitefish"])

```

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|  - input_species2
fish |> 
  filter(Species == input_species2) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = 
           aes(x = Length1, 
               y = Weight)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y~x)+
  labs(
    title = "Scatterplot of Weight and Length of Fish With Linear Models",
    x = "Length (cm)",
    y = "Weight (grams)"
  )
```

We can then have students examine a linear model and discuss. 1. For what species does the linear model accurately represent? 2. What does the slope mean in the context of the problem? 3. What does the y-intercept mean in the context of the problem? 4. Does the y-intercept make logical sense? 5. Does the line fit the model appropriately?

### Part 3: Next, we will examine polynomial trend lines.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof input_species3 = Inputs.select(["Perch", "Bream", "Roach", "Pike", "Smelt", "Parkki", "Whitefish"])

```

```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|  - input_species3
fish <- read_csv("fish.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fish |> 
  filter(Species == input_species3) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = 
           aes(x = Length1, 
               y = Weight)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = 'loess', se = FALSE, formula = y~x)+
  labs(
    title = "Scatterplot of Weight and Length of Fish With Linear Models",
    x = "Length (cm)",
    y = "Weight (grams)"
  )
```

Next, we can show students a polynomial trend line and discuss.

1.  How does this trend line compare to the linear trend line?
2.  Can we predict the length of a fish by using its weight?

### Part 4: Transformed Variables

Students can also explore whether transforming a variable can make the relationship appear more linear. We can create new columns for (Length\^2) and (Length\^3), and plot the weight against each transformed variable. Students can compare the transformed graphs with the original plot and discuss which model looks more linear.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof input_species4 = Inputs.select(["Perch", "Bream", "Roach", "Pike", "Smelt", "Parkki", "Whitefish"])

```

::::: {layout="[50, 50]"}
::: {#squared-column}
```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - input_species4

fish |>
  filter(Species == input_species4) |>
  mutate(
    Length1_squared = Length1^2
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Length1_squared, y = Weight)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              se = FALSE,
              formula = y ~ poly(x, 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Weight vs. Length Squared",
    x = "Length² (cm²)",
    y = "Weight (grams)"
  )
```
:::

::: {}
```{webr}
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - input_species4

fish |>
  filter(Species == input_species4) |>
  mutate(
    Length1_cubed = Length1^3
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Length1_cubed, y = Weight)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              se = FALSE, 
              formula = y ~ poly(x, 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Weight vs. Length Cubed",
    x = "Length³ (cm³)",
    y = "Weight (grams)"
  )
```
:::
:::::

1.  Does plotting weight against (Length\^2) or (Length\^3) change the pattern?
2.  Which graph appears to be the most linear?
3.  Does a more linear graph make the predictions easier or more accurate?
4.  Take note of which species of fish work well with the two different transformations.


## Ethics and Equity Prompt

Students identify the observed range of lengths and predict weights inside and outside that range. They label predictions as interpolation or extrapolation and explain why extrapolation can be misleading.

## Conclusion

After this lesson, students should now understand that functions can model relationships in the real world, and help us make predictions. Linear and quadratic models are simple examples of the types of models that can be used with machine learning. However, not all models are good models and are only approximations, so they may not always be accurate or make sense outside of the context of our data.
